opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's a pretty natural consequence of where the best open-weight models are coming from right now. If you're a startup in the U.S. and you've decided to build on open models, whether to fine-tune them, distill from them, or run them on your own infrastructure for cost or privacy reasons, the honest reality is that many of the strongest options over the last year or so have come out of Chinese labs. Qwen, DeepSeek, Kimi from Moonshot, GLM from Zhipu, MiniMax. These are the models people actually download and build on, and you can see it in the Hugging Face numbers and in what startups quietly tell you they're using under the hood.

Once your product depends on a model family, you want a relationship with the people making it. You want to know what's coming in the next release, whether they'll keep the license permissive, whether a new architecture will break your inference stack, what the post-training recipe looked like so you can extend it without wrecking the model. You want to give feedback, like "your tool use is flaky in this setting" or "we need a smaller dense version." That's how it works with any upstream dependency in open source. If the key maintainers of your core library are in Hangzhou or Beijing, eventually someone gets on a plane.

The Chinese labs also have a real incentive to welcome that. Open weights are a big part of how they build global mindshare and an ecosystem, especially when they can't always compete on closed API distribution in the West. Having American companies building on Qwen or DeepSeek is a win for them, so I'd expect them to be pretty receptive.

The tension, and part of why I keep talking about this, is that it's happening while the U.S. still doesn't have a strong, consistently released set of open models at the frontier. That's the motivation behind efforts like ATOM and the push for more American open models. If American companies are building on Chinese open models and forming ties with Chinese labs, that's not necessarily bad in itself, since a lot of it is just normal scientific and engineering exchange, but it's a signal about where the center of gravity in open models is. If we care about having influence over the standards, the safety practices, and the research direction in open AI, we need to be producing the models people want to build on, not just consuming them. So I see these relationships forming as a market outcome and a bit of a warning sign about the gap the U.S. has left open.

r001.rationale: The response says U.S. startups seek relationships to learn about releases, licenses, architectures, and post-training recipes, and says Chinese labs may welcome them. It does not clearly state that the labs’ willingness to share technical knowledge motivates those relationships.

r002.rationale: The response mentions someone getting on a plane but does not compare entry barriers for Americans visiting China with those for Chinese researchers or engineers visiting the United States.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the simplest version is that if you're a startup and your entire product is built on top of a model, you eventually need to know the people who make that model. Right now, the best open-weight models are mostly coming out of China: Qwen, DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, MiniMax. If you're fine-tuning on those, serving them, building agents on them, you have questions. Why did this behavior change between versions? What's on the roadmap? Can you give me a heads-up before the next release so I'm not scrambling the day it drops? Those are normal supplier relationships, and you can't get them by reading a GitHub README.

American labs have mostly stepped back from this. Meta's commitment to open weights looks a lot shakier than it did a year or two ago. OpenAI put out some open models, and that's great, but it's not the center of their business. So if you're a US company and you're serious about open models as your foundation, the gravity pulls you toward the groups that are actually shipping at the frontier, and those teams are in Hangzhou and Beijing and Shanghai.

I'd expect this to look a lot like what happened in semiconductors or hardware over the past couple decades. You go visit the supplier. You sit in a room with the engineers. You build trust, you learn how they think about releases, and over time you get a little bit of influence over what they build, because they want adoption in the US market too. That's a two-way relationship. Chinese labs benefit enormously from American developers using their models, because it's distribution, it's feedback, it's legitimacy.

Now, there's obviously tension here. There's geopolitical pressure, there's export control politics, there are real questions about dependencies. I'm not saying it's uncomplicated. But I think the pull is strong enough that it's going to happen regardless. People who build on open models are pragmatic. They go where the weights are, and the weights are coming from China. So I'd expect, over the next year or two, you'll see more founders making those trips, more quiet collaborations, and frankly more American companies realizing they'd rather have a relationship than just be a downstream consumer with no visibility.

r001.rationale: The response says startups seek roadmap information, release updates, and contact with engineers, but it does not communicate that Chinese labs’ willingness to share technical knowledge motivates those relationships.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare the ease of Americans visiting China with the difficulty of Chinese researchers or engineers visiting the United States.

astra-6.text:
Because if you’re building your company on top of a model from a Chinese lab, that lab is now an important part of your supply chain. You want to understand what they’re working on, when the next model is coming, and whether the things you need are priorities for them. You can download the weights without knowing anyone, but that doesn’t replace having a relationship with the people building the model.

And the incentives go both ways. The startup wants better models and some visibility into the roadmap. The lab wants people using its models and giving useful feedback. So I’d expect some founders to go meet those teams. It’s a pretty natural consequence of Chinese open models becoming useful foundations for American businesses.

sol-6.1.text:
Because if you’re building your company on top of a model from a Chinese lab, that lab is effectively one of your most important technology partners. The weights are open, so you don’t need a relationship to get started. But you still want to know: What are they training next? What capabilities are they prioritizing? How is the license going to evolve? And if you find a problem, who can you talk to?

There’s value for the labs, too. American startups can give them feedback about how their models perform in real products and what developers actually need. So I expect some of these relationships to develop pretty naturally. If a team is producing the best open model for your use case, at some point you want to meet the people building it—even if that means getting on a plane to China.

r001.rationale: The response says the open weights let startups get started without a relationship and that a relationship offers insight into future training, priorities, licensing, and support. It does not say Chinese labs share technical knowledge as the motivating factor.

r002.rationale: The response mentions getting on a plane to China, but makes no comparison between entry barriers for Americans visiting China and Chinese researchers or engineers visiting the United States.
